new_statements.quote: He believes it is due to "stress uncertainty" as a result of a tendency towards columnar stress (pp. 234-8). This tendency is evident in the nominative plural aθróp(i) instead of inherited áθrop(i) and abounds in the agglutinative inflection of proparoxytone nouns with violation of the three-syllable rule, e.g. jáskaloz-ju and jáskaloz-ja at Ghurzono (13), áropoz-ju and áropoz-ja at Aravan (13), átropoz-ju, átropoz-ja and átropoz-ja-ju at Ulağaç (20). There is, however, no evidence whatsoever of stress uncertainty in the genitive singular in Cappadocian, where forms such as *áθrop(u) instead of inherited aθróp(u) are not attested.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog record for Cappadocian has an empty rule; this work adds that stress is lexically fixed per stem (Greek stress classes) with a columnar tendency and no three-syllable window in agglutinative forms. Consistent with Kooij & Revithiadou 2001.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A morphology chapter, not a phonology; stress is treated only incidentally through the inherited Greek lexical stress classes (oxytone, paroxytone, proparoxytone nouns, each inflecting differently). It reports (after Karatsareas 2011) a tendency toward columnar (stem-fixed) stress in the agglutinative inflection, so that proparoxytone nouns keep their stem stress and end up with preantepenultimate stress (lípsandoz-ja, jáskaloz-ju), i.e. the Greek three-syllable window is not respected; the inherited genitive singular -jú is stressed on the final syllable for oxytone nouns and derives from a shift of penultimate to ultimate stress (-íu > -jú); p. 12 notes Axo forms 'noteworthy for their preantepenultimate stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts in the inherited fusional paradigm (áθropos, pl. aθrópi, gen. aθrópu) versus columnar stress in the agglutinative paradigm (áropoz-ju, áropoz-ja); paroxytone kinship terms keep penultimate stress in the vocative (p. 41); all facts are village-specific (Axo, Aravan, Ghurzono, Ulağaç, Misti, Fertek, Semendere).
new_statements.identity_note: Kooij & Revithiadou 2001 (data from Dawkins 1916) divide Cappadocian into three groups: (a) Delmeso and Potámia, (b) Axo, Mistí, Aravan, (c) Ulaghatsh and Semenderé; the quoted p. 96 statement is about group (a), the final-default statement (p. 105) about groups (b) and (c); the paper also treats Pontic, which is a different variety (compositional accentuation, not covered here). Janse 2019 draws on many villages (Axo, Misti, Aravan, Ulağaç, Ghurzono, Fertek, Semendere, Malakopi) and describes contemporary Mišótika as well as Dawkins-era data.

new_statements.quote: With respect to stress, the dialects are lexical accent systems. At first sight, stress can occur anywhere in a word and syllable structure plays no role in determining its exact position. There is a strong preference for final stress perhaps due to the vast presence of Turkish words. No convincing evidence in support of trochees was found. [...] Unlike Greek and Pontic, the resolution of accent competition is edge-oriented: when accents compete, the rightmost one wins. In the absence of accents, we must agree that word prominence is initial because words like δjávolos and áθropos, composed of unaccented morphemes, have initial stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has Cappadocian with an empty rule; this is the dedicated accentuation study and supplies the type (lexical accent, unbounded, two edge-based cophonologies with initial vs final defaults). Nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Cappadocian is a lexical-accent system: morphemes (roots and suffixes) are lexically accented, pre-accenting, post-accenting or unaccented, so stress position is unpredictable from phonology, and there is no syllable-count window (stress is unbounded, e.g. ráftsiniwka, erxútomeste). In fusional (Greek-type) words the rightmost lexical accent wins and, with no accent, default stress is initial (áθropos, δjávolos). In hybrid and agglutinating words (and Turkish loans) the default is final, following the Turkish rule, and the leftmost accent wins in competition (p. 105: 'We propose that the default accentuation in A- and H-type words is final, in total compliance to the Turkish stress rule.. When two competing accents meet in a word, the leftmost one wins.'). Group c dialects (Ulaghatsh, Semenderé) use only the Turkish-type cophonology (final default).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Cappadocian; the authors say only that 'No convincing evidence in support of trochees was found' (p. 96).
new_statements.exceptions: Two cophonologies coexist: fusional words (rightmost accent wins, initial default) vs hybrid/agglutinating words and Turkish loans (leftmost accent wins, final default); pre-accenting suffix /-ˊja/ gives penultimate stress in nom/acc.pl (qarɨ́δja, güzélja); only finally stressed nom/acc.sg forms show mobile stress in gen.sg (p. 105); word-final unstressed /i, u/ delete in all dialects (fn. 16).
new_statements.identity_note: Kooij & Revithiadou 2001 (data from Dawkins 1916) divide Cappadocian into three groups: (a) Delmeso and Potámia, (b) Axo, Mistí, Aravan, (c) Ulaghatsh and Semenderé; the quoted p. 96 statement is about group (a), the final-default statement (p. 105) about groups (b) and (c); the paper also treats Pontic, which is a different variety (compositional accentuation, not covered here). Janse 2019 draws on many villages (Axo, Misti, Aravan, Ulağaç, Ghurzono, Fertek, Semendere, Malakopi) and describes contemporary Mišótika as well as Dawkins-era data.
